newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION-SAfrica labour standards - By Vishwas Satgar.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-SAfrica labour standards - By Vishwas Satgar.

text.p: By Vishwas Satgar, policy analyst and researcher at the National Labour and Economic Development Institute (NALEDI)
JOHANNESBURG, Aug 14 - If former South African Communist Party leader Chris Hani were alive he most certainly would have been at the forefront of labour's employment mass action campaign.

More probably though, given his principled commitment to workers, he would have intervened much earlier in the negotiations process and secured an agreement from government, most favourable to labour.
Unfortunately, Hani was assassinated and the reality prevailing in the employment standards negotiations is very different. It has been protracted and embroiled in a volatile impasse.
In this context it would seem the options for labour range from a bargained compromise to a defeat.
Prompting this have been commentators who have suggested labour is behaving most naively and spoiling the miracle of South Africa's transition to democracy.
Business, on the other hand, has been fairly divided yet still oppositional.

Some elements have argued consistently for "Thatcherite" deregulation and flexibility in the labour market, while more recently, moderate voices have been proposing a case for basic employment standards but not "best practice" standards.
The policy thrust of this business position is the balancing of growth and employment with "equitable" labour market conditions.

Ultimately, the labour market policy outcome envisaged is: more jobs but low quality jobs. In other words the business elite of this country, the main beneficiaries of apartheid, want to stabilise poverty but not eradicate it.

Notwithstanding the barrage of criticism against labour and the narrowing of options, it has stood firm in its commitment to a well thought out and intelligent policy approach to employment standards reform.
It would seem there are three policy premises to labour's reform proposals:

(i) "Best practice" in South Africa was and is the result of a flexible labour market in which basic conditions were not even achieved by most workers including organised workers, in some sectors, primarily because the regulatory institutions and instruments did not provide the necessary enforcement for the basic standards to be basic legal entitlements.
At the same time the flexibility in dismissal laws allowed business to use the surplus supply of unemployed labour to undercut the standards of organised workers;
(ii) Structural transformation of the South African economy, in the context of "globalisation," is not incompatible with improved labour standards.

It is more likely that an improvement in labour market institutions and standards (like a modernised wage board, reduced working hours, higher overtime rates, double pay for Sunday work, higher prohibitory thresholds for child labour and so on) facilitate the realisation of social policy ends and the promotion of economic efficiencies at micro and macro levels of the economy;
(iii) Although improved labour standards would increase labour costs this would not necessarily have an inhibitory effect on job creation.
The increased value of labour could have multiplier effects through the economy, which could stimulate employment and even growth.

Similarly in its substantive reform proposals, labour has not been self seeking and reflexive but rational. A good example is six months paid maternity leave, which has been opposed mainly on the ground that it would create a disincentive for the employment of women.

In the first instance, for labour it is apparent six months maternity leave is not new to South Africa. With the maternity benefits in the Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) white middle class women mainly acquired maternity leave for a six month duration.
Secondly, it is sexist to assume that six months maternity leave would suddenly prompt a demographic explosion - women are just going to fall pregnant.

Accompanying this sexist assertion is a blindness to the fact that women have recourse to an abortion law and other reproductive technologies that have and are enabling them to assert an autonomy over reproduction.

Thirdly, the constitution has far-reaching anti-discrimination provisions and buttressing this within the labour market is the Labour Relations Act (LRA) of 1995 which has a reach even at the point of entry of employment, through the particular definition of the unfair labour practice concept.
Fourthly, the real issue at stake is the cost of maternity leave. For labour this primarily relates to full cost or pay for maternity leave, at least for four months.

In this regard it would seem as though labour has been willing to contemplate a set of feasible formulas from a special maternity fund, funded through levies on all employers and employees to the use of a reformed UIF.

Notwithstanding the realism and feasibility of labour's negotiating agenda, it has tragically come up against a government which is obsessed with managing perceptions of foreign investors and local business.

It has displayed a lack of will to govern according to it's alliance and electoral mandate - the Reconstruction and Development Programme - which was not obtained from Business South Africa or the business capitals of the world but from the two million strong Congress of South African Trade Unions, members of the African National Congress and the South African Communist Party.
Essentially a constituency the government hopes would vote it back into power in 1999.

With a vacillating government informed by a confused conception of "pragmatic neutrality" which has both placated business and contributed to its increased intransigence, labour's approach to the impasse in the Basic Employment Standards negotiation has to be decisive - either at the National Economic Development and Labour Council or parliament.
This means labour needs to set its sights on a strategic solution that is transformative and does not insulate the law from change and challenge.
In this sense labour should try and achieve an outcome which consolidates gains made in the law but at the same time is neither a compromise nor labour defeat.
This means labour has to recognise legal reform of the labour market is not a once off event.
For instance, even after the Labour Relations Act was negotiated successive changes have been made to it, although mainly emanating from government in order to fine-tune the law.

Similarly, this does not prevent labour from proactively demanding and asserting amendments to the Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA) in the future or making demands for improved standards to the employment standards commission or using organisational strategies that would improve on the basic standards.

Alternatively expressed, the BCEA negotiations needs to be understood as producing a challenge to labour to struggle to deepen legal reform and ultimately benefits for the poor working population of this country.
However, the only uncertainty in this strategic approach is:
Will South African democracy be able to handle it?

Put differently, will this government and future governments respect the rights and freedoms of labour to organise and struggle for better employment conditions and ultimately a better society for all?
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
